--- Slide/Halaman 3 ---
an increase in temperature speeds up cellular chemical  reactions,  
whereas  a  decrease  in  temperature  slows  down these reactions.
Because cell function is sensitive to fluctuations in  internal  temperature,  
humans  homeostatically maintain body temperature at a level optimal for 
stable cellular metabolism


--- Slide/Halaman 4 ---
Body Core Temperature 
and  Skin  Temperature
Normal  body  temperature  taken  orally  (by  mouth): 98.6°F (37°C).
normal  body  temperature  varies  among individuals and varies 
throughout the day, ranging from 96.0°F (35.5°C) in the morning to 99.9°F 
(37.7°C) in the evening, with an overall average of 98.2°F (36.7°C)
internal core temperature is subject to precise regulation to maintain its 
homeostatic constancy. The core tissues function best at a relatively 
constant temperature of around 100°F (37.8°C)
skin temperature may fluctuate between 68°F and 104°F (20°C and 40°C) 
without damage. The temperature of the skin is deliberately varied as a 
control measure to help maintain the core’s thermal constancy


--- Slide/Halaman 5 ---
Estimated range of body “core” 
temperature in normal people


--- Slide/Halaman 6 ---
Sites  for  monitoring  body  
temperature
The oral and axillary temperatures are comparable, whereas rectal 
temperature averages about 1°F (0.56°C) higher
temperature-monitoring  instrument that scans the heat generated by the 
eardrum
temporal scanner that measures the temperature of the blood in 
the temporal artery


--- Slide/Halaman 7 ---
Heat Production
(1) basal rate of metabolism of all the cells of the body; 
(2)  extra  rate  of  metabolism  caused  by  muscle  activity
(3) extra  metabolism  caused  by  the  effect  of  thyroxine, growth hormone 
and testosterone on the cells; 
(4) extra metabolism caused by the effect of epinephrine, norepinephrine, 
and sympathetic stimulation on the cells; 
(5) extra metabolism caused by increased chemical activity in the cells  
themselves,  especially  when  the  cell  temperature increases;  
(6)  extra  metabolism  needed  for  digestion, absorption, and storage of food 
(thermogenic effect of food).


--- Slide/Halaman 8 ---
Heat Loss
(1)  how  rapidly  heat  can  be  conducted from where it is produced in the 
body core to the skin 
(2) how rapidly heat can then be transferred from the skin to the surroundings.


--- Slide/Halaman 9 ---
Insulator System of the Body
The skin, the subcutaneous tissues, and especially the fat of the 
subcutaneous tissues act together as a heat  insulator for the body.
The insulation beneath the skin is an effective means of  maintaining  
normal  internal  core  temperature,  even though it allows the temperature 
of the skin to approach the temperature of the surroundings


--- Slide/Halaman 10 ---
Heat input must balance
heat output
to
maintain a stablecore temperature


--- Slide/Halaman 11 ---
The body uses four mechanisms of heat transfer: 
radiation, conduction, convection,and evaporation


--- Slide/Halaman 12 ---


--- Slide/Halaman 13 ---
Major
thermoregulatory pathways.


--- Slide/Halaman 14 ---
Sweating is an active evaporative heat-loss process under sympathetic 
nervous control
Shivering is the primary involuntary means of increasing heat production
a rise in core temperature caused by  heat  exposure—two  mechanisms  
reduce  heat-producing skeletal muscle activity: Muscle tone is reflexly
decreased, and voluntary movement is curtailed
Nonshivering thermogenesis  is  mediated  on  cold  exposure  by  the  
sympathetic nervous system, which increases heat production by 
stimulating brown fat,a special type of adipose tissue that is especially 
capable of converting chemical energy from food into heat


--- Slide/Halaman 15 ---
The mitochondria of brown fat contain a unique uncoupling protein called 
thermogenin(“heat producer”)
adult brown fat becomes more active on cold exposure
The amount of heat lost to the environment by radiation and the 
conduction–convection process is largely determined by the temperature 
gradient between the skin and the external environment. 


--- Slide/Halaman 16 ---
To  maintain  a  constant  core  temperature,  the  insulative capacity and 
temperature of the skin can be adjusted
skin vasomotor responses are coordinated by the hypothalamus  by  means  
of  sympathetic  nervous  system  output


--- Slide/Halaman 17 ---
Coordinated Adjustments in Response 
to Cold or Heat Exposure


--- Slide/Halaman 18 ---
Fever production


--- Slide/Halaman 19 ---
heat stroke
extremely dangerous situation that arises from the complete breakdown of 
the hypothalamic thermoregulatory systems. 
Heat stroke is more likely to occur on overexertion during a prolonged 
exposure to a hot, humid environment. 
The  elderly,  in  whom  thermoregulatory  responses  are generally slower 
and less efficient, are particularly vulnerable to heat stroke  during  
prolonged,  stifling  heat  waves.  
individuals who are taking certain common tranquilizers, such as Valium, 
because these  drugs  interfere  with  the  hypothalamic  thermoregulatory  
centers’ neurotransmitter activity
